ACIG: Growth companies outside the US, picked by Hartford's managers to beat the standard international growth yardstick. The hand-picked approach concentrates on firms seen as the strongest growers abroad, accepting the extra swing that comes with growth styles and foreign markets.
BFJL: Bitcoin with a floor under it: over the period starting in July, it is designed to stop losses at about 15 percent while capping how much of bitcoin's gains it keeps. It suits investors who want bitcoin exposure with a hard limit on the downside.
BROL: Large US growth companies, led by technology at a bit over a third, chosen by Baron with an eye on limiting big drawdowns. It aims to keep growth investing's upside while softening its worst falls, a balance most growth funds do not attempt.
CAPA: Makers of capacitors, the tiny parts that store and smooth electric charge inside every AI server and data center. It is a narrow bet on an unglamorous but essential corner of the AI build-out, so it rises and falls with chip spending.
COMD: Commodities of all kinds: oil, metals and farm goods, reached through futures and similar contracts under active management. It can diversify a stock and bond portfolio since raw materials often move on their own cycle, though commodity prices are famously volatile.
DACL: Derivatives that follow an index of autocallable notes, structured products on stock markets that pay steady income and can end early when markets behave. The defensive design aims to soften falls, but the income comes with capped gains and note-style complexity.
DIVH: Dividend-paying stocks gathered for income, spread across technology, banks, energy and everyday consumer brands. It aims to harvest a steady stream of dividends from many industries at once, favoring reliable payers over chasing the single highest yields.
DPRE: Real estate income from several sources: property-owning trusts, preferred shares and real estate company debt. Mixing stock-like and bond-like real estate payers aims for higher, steadier income than a plain REIT fund, though property downturns still hurt.
DUKX: A tactical fund that moves between international stock funds and cash, following market trends to decide how much risk to take. When foreign markets look weak it can sit in cash, which can miss snap-back rallies but aims to dodge deep falls.
DUTY: US companies earning at least half their money from defense: weapons platforms, military technology, logistics and cybersecurity, split between tech and industrial names. It is a focused bet on Pentagon spending, moving with defense budgets more than the wider economy.
EPMV: Mid-sized US companies that look undervalued, spread across industrials, banks, technology and consumer firms. Harbor's managers pick them by hand, aiming for the middle of the market at reasonable prices, so it can lag when expensive growth stocks run.
EPSB: Small and mid-sized US companies across industrials, technology, banks and health care, picked by Harbor's managers as a core holding. It covers the market's middleweights and up-and-comers in one fund, with more swing than large-company funds but more substance than microcaps.
ETCO: An options strategy on an ether fund, built to squeeze high income out of the second-largest cryptocurrency while keeping some exposure to its price. Selling options caps the upside, and ether's deep drops can still bite through the income.
ETEC: Companies building breakthrough fixes for climate change: clean technology, environmental engineering and new energy ideas across industrials and tech. It is a growth bet on climate innovation rather than steady utilities, so it swings with funding and policy moods.
FEMD: Mid-sized US companies bought with First Eagle's value approach, hunting for solid businesses priced below their worth. The patient, bargain-first style aims to protect against big losses while mid-caps compound, so it may trail in hot growth markets.
FESC: Small US companies bought with a value mindset: profitable little firms bought at prices the managers see as bargains. First Eagle's patient, bargain-hunting style sets it apart, aiming to lose less in downturns while small caps grow over time.
GLDN: Gold industry companies, mostly miners, combined with options sold on them and on gold funds to generate income. It aims to pay regular income from the gold business rather than just ride the metal's price, though miners still swing hard.
HBIT: Bitcoin exposure with an active hedge: managers can pull back into cash-like safety when their risk signals warn of trouble. That sets it apart from plain bitcoin funds, trading some upside in strong runs for smaller falls in bad ones.
IGGY: Growth companies outside the US, spread across at least three countries and led by technology and industrial firms in equal measure. AllianceBernstein's managers pick the stocks actively, so it is a bet on their favorite foreign growers rather than a market index.
IND: India's 500 biggest traded companies in one fund, led by banks at about 30 percent, with consumer, industrial and materials firms behind. It is a broad bet on India's growth story, carrying the currency and political swings of a single emerging market.
IOYY: An income strategy using derivatives on a leveraged fund tied to IonQ, a quantum computing company, harvesting its extreme price swings as payouts. Few income funds are riskier: leverage resets, option caps and a speculative underlying stock can combine into steep losses.
JADB: Large US stocks wrapped in a deep options cushion, set up each January to absorb a large share of any market fall over the following year. The protection costs upside, since gains are limited, so it targets cautious investors fearing a bad year.
JHAC: US companies of every size, from giants to small firms, researched one by one and weighted by business fundamentals rather than market price. It is a core stock holding with a built-in tilt away from whatever happens to be most expensive.
LFAI: US Treasury bonds arranged to pay a regular income meant to last through 2055, funding spending late into life. It is built for very long retirements: steady government-backed payments for decades, though its distant horizon means prices move with interest rates.
MUND: Tax-exempt municipal bonds in a long ladder reaching to 2055, paying federal-tax-free interest in distributions as the rungs mature. It is built for savers planning spending in the mid 2050s who want steady income the tax man mostly leaves alone.
NVOH: A single-stock fund holding the US-listed shares of Novo Nordisk, the Danish drug maker behind famous diabetes and weight loss treatments. A currency hedge softens swings between the krone and the dollar, leaving returns riding on one pharma giant.
OBOR: Companies positioned to benefit from China's Belt and Road building program across Asia, Africa and beyond, led by banks, materials and industrial firms. It is a bet on Chinese-led infrastructure spending, with the political and currency risks that follow it.
OCDB: Large US stocks wrapped in a deep options cushion, set up each October to absorb a large share of a market fall over the following year. In return, gains are limited, making it a defensive pick for investors bracing for trouble.
ODDS: Digital entertainment companies worldwide: video game makers, streaming services and esports firms, split between media and consumer stocks. It is a focused bet on how people play and watch now, riding game releases, subscribers and advertising.
ORO: A tactical mix that shifts between bitcoin futures, gold futures and cash, guided by computer models watching price trends. It aims to catch much of bitcoin's rises with fewer of its crashes, though the signals can whipsaw in choppy markets.
PLA: A note-like bet on Palantir stock built from derivatives rather than shares, designed to pay income while the stock holds up or rises. If Palantir falls hard, the fund can drop sharply too, and steady payouts come with a ceiling on gains.
PMOC: The S&P 500's big US companies, combined with an options cushion over the one-year period starting in October. The cushion absorbs the opening slice of a fall while capping gains, so it is built for a smoother stock market ride.
PWRX: Power and infrastructure companies: utilities, energy firms and the industrial builders behind the grid, in roughly equal thirds. It is an actively managed bet on the world's electricity build-out, with an income-friendly tilt from steady infrastructure cash flows.
QQI: One hundred innovative companies from outside the US, chosen from the Nasdaq stable of growth names, led by technology and health care. It is the international cousin of the famous Nasdaq 100 approach, so it leans into growth and swings harder than broad foreign funds.
RTOO: Robotics companies: the makers of factory robots, warehouse automation and the technology behind them, led by industrials at about 60 percent. It is a growth bet on machines doing more of the world's physical work, a fast-moving and sometimes frothy theme.
SBB: A short-term trading tool that rises when small US companies fall, resetting its inverse bet every day. The daily reset steadily erodes returns over longer periods, so it suits brief bearish trades rather than a lasting hedge.
TEST: Synthetic exposure to Tesla stock plus an options program targeting a 25 percent yearly payout rate. The distributions ride on Tesla's wild price swings, so the fund itself is extremely jumpy, and the option strategy limits gains when Tesla surges.
TMDV: Companies that have raised their dividends every year for at least 35 years, drawn from across the US market and led by everyday consumer brands, industrials and banks. That long record makes it a steady income holding, heavy on mature firms rather than fast growers.
TPRY: US stocks picked with a contrarian streak, favoring companies beaten down when markets throw a tantrum, led by technology at about half the fund. It pairs that bargain hunting with a strategy targeting 15 percent yearly payouts, a bold income goal.
TXUG: Growth companies in developed markets outside the US, led by technology at a bit over a third, with industrials behind. Thornburg's managers pick each stock for its growth prospects, so it is an actively run bet on foreign growers rather than an index copy.
UBEW: A weekly-reset strategy on Uber, the ride-hailing company, using swaps and shares to magnify its weekly moves a little while paying weekly distributions. The weekly reset makes it a trading tool, not a holding: in choppy weeks the magnification works against it.
USIN: US Treasury bonds with seven to ten years left before they mature, held in equal rungs across those years like a ladder. The ladder design spreads interest-rate risk, giving steady government income with moderate price swings when rates move.
UX: Uranium exposure in two forms: derivatives tied to the price of uranium itself, plus shares of companies that mine it and trusts that hold it. It is a focused bet on nuclear fuel, an extremely jumpy market driven by energy politics and reactor demand.
VEEM: Emerging-market companies that stock analysts are most positive about, led by technology at close to half the fund. It tilts the usual emerging-market mix toward analyst favorites, adding their judgment to markets already known for sharp swings.
VEFA: Developed-market companies outside the US that stock analysts are most upbeat about, led by banks at a bit over a quarter. It tilts a standard international portfolio toward Wall Street's favorite names, so it leans on analyst opinion as its stock picker.
VGRO: Large US companies picked for above-average growth, with technology close to half the fund and media and internet firms behind. Silvant's managers hunt durable growers, so it leans into the market's strongest earners and swings more than a plain large-company fund.
XDAT: Companies riding the flood of data: the firms storing, moving and processing the world's information, with technology about 70 percent and media firms behind. It is a growth bet on data use exploding, a theme powered by AI and cloud computing.
XDEF: European defense technology companies: weapons makers, space firms and cybersecurity specialists, with industrials over 90 percent of the fund. It is a focused bet on Europe rearming, moving with government military budgets and security worries.
XUSM: Companies outside the US whose share prices have been rising strongly, picked by momentum across the previous months and led by banks. Momentum funds ride winners and drop losers, which can work well in trends but whipsaws when markets reverse suddenly.
YXI: A short-term trading tool that rises when the 50 biggest Chinese companies listed in Hong Kong fall, resetting its bet every day. The daily reset makes it drift over longer stretches, so it is built for brief bearish bets, not holding.
